Iron-based materials possess biocompatibility and biodegradability advantages over other transition metals for EMI shielding applications.
The total shielding effectiveness equation is SET = SER + SEA + SEM, where contributions from secondary reflections (SEM) can be neglected when SEA > 10 dB.
Reflection loss (SER) decreases with increasing frequency for constant conductivity and permeability values.
In non-magnetic materials, shielding is mainly governed by reflection, while in magnetic conducting metals, shielding is dominated by absorption.
Ferromagnetic materials have an intrinsic cutoff frequency usually below the low GHz range, limiting their broadband EMI shielding capability.
Nano- and micro-sized materials lower eddy current losses compared to bulk ferromagnetic materials.

Larger Fe₃O₄ nanoparticles improve electrical conductivity by boosting graphitization of the carbon matrix.
Complex permittivity is expressed as ε = ε' + iε'', where ε' is energy storage capacity and ε'' relates to dielectric losses.
Complex permeability is expressed as μ = μ' + iμ'', where μ' is magnetic energy storage and μ'' relates to ohmic losses.
Impedance matching occurs when input impedance equals free space impedance (Z₀ = 377 Ω), maximizing microwave absorption.
The 1/4 wavelength equation (tm = nc/4fm√(3μ)) is used to design absorbers with broad effective absorption bandwidth.
Reflection loss minimum (RLmin) of -20 dB is considered 99% microwave absorption according to standard definitions.
Skin depth δ = (fμσ)^(-1/2) represents the thickness where incident field attenuates to 1/e of initial value.
Porous and hollow structures provide large surface areas and vacant spaces for scattering and multiple reflection of EM waves.
The Maxwell-Wagner effect occurs at multi-interfaces where bound charges accumulate, enhancing electromagnetic attenuation.
Heat treatment creates defects (vacancies, dangling bonds) that enhance attenuation rather than reflection in ferrite systems.
Dielectric loss is given by ε'' = σ/2πε₀, indicating that high electrical conductivity enhances dielectric loss.
At high frequencies (above 100 MHz), only the spin rotational component remains in complex permeability; domain wall motion contribution diminishes.
Percolation threshold depends on filler shape, morphology, aspect ratio, and volume fraction in composite materials.

Anisotropy field Ha = 2K/μ₀Ms, where K is anisotropy constant and Ms is saturation magnetization.
Natural resonance frequency fr = γHa/2π, where γ/2π is the gyromagnetic ratio.
Snoek's limit fr(μ-1) ∝ fMs establishes a boundary on microwave permeability spectrum in magnetic materials.
